name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MICROBESINHUMANWELFARE_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Labelled parts of a typical biogas plant

questiontext.text: The given schematic represents a typical biogas plant. Identify the parts labelled A, B, C, and D.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic shows an underground concrete tank system with an inlet chamber on the left (A), an inverted floating cylindrical drum at the top (B) containing gases such as \(\text{CH}_4\) and \(\text{CO}_2\), a deep central underground tank (C), and a side outlet chamber on the right (D).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The diagram represents a standard floating-cover anaerobic biogas plant (developed in India by IARI and KVIC), where substrate enters from one side, undergoes anaerobic digestion in the central tank, and spent residue exits on the opposite side.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Methanogenic bacteria (such as Methanobacterium) act anaerobically on cellulosic bio-wastes and cattle dung slurry in the digester to produce biogas (predominantly methane along with \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Part A is the inlet tank where cattle dung and water are mixed into a slurry and fed into the plant.
2. Part C is the deep concrete digester tank (10–15 feet deep) where anaerobic microbial digestion occurs.
3. Part B is the floating gas-holder placed over the slurry, which rises as biogas accumulates and supplies gas through the top outlet pipe.
4. Part D is the outlet tank where spent slurry (sludge) is collected for use as fertiliser.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking the flow direction from inlet to digester to gas-holder and spent sludge outlet confirms all four assignments are biologically and structurally consistent. Therefore, A is the dung and water slurry inlet, B is the gas-holder, C is the digester, and D is the spent sludge outlet.

answer.text: A: Spent sludge outlet, B: Digester, C: Gas-holder, D: Dung and water slurry inlet
A: Dung and water slurry inlet, B: Gas-holder, C: Digester, D: Spent sludge outlet
A: Gas-holder, B: Dung and water slurry inlet, C: Spent sludge outlet, D: Digester
A: Dung and water slurry inlet, B: Digester, C: Gas-holder, D: Spent sludge outlet

questiontext.text: Observe the given diagram of a bacteriophage and identify the parts labelled P, Q, R, and S.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram depicts a virus that infects bacteria (a bacteriophage), with four structures marked from top to bottom as P, Q, R, and S.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The schematic follows the standard NCERT representation of a bacteriophage showing its external proteinaceous architecture.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A bacteriophage consists of a polyhedral head housing genetic material, a short neck/collar region, a helical tail sheath, a basal plate with pins, and elongated prongs (tail fibres) for attachment to the bacterial host.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. P points to the upper hexagonal/polyhedral structure, which is the Head.
2. Q points to the segmented region immediately below the head, which is the Collar.
3. R points to the central cylindrical shaft below the collar, which is the Tail.
4. S points to the leg-like appendages extending from the base plate, which are the Prongs.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Matching each label from top to bottom gives P as Head, Q as Collar, R as Tail, and S as Prongs.

answer.text: P: Head, Q: Tail, R: Collar, S: Plate
P: Collar, Q: Head, R: Plate, S: Prongs
P: Head, Q: Plate, R: Tail, S: Pins
P: Head, Q: Collar, R: Tail, S: Prongs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MICROBESINHUMANWELFARE_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Identification of bacteria and viruses by morphology

questiontext.text: Identify the micro-organisms represented by (I), (II), and (III) in the given schematic figures.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Three distinct microbial morphologies are shown: (I) a single cylindrical/rod-shaped cell with long wavy flagella, (II) a polyhedral/icosahedral particle lacking a tail, and (III) elongated, compact rod-shaped viral particles.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The schematics represent standard bacterial and viral morphologies described in the chapter (magnified at 50,000X for the flagellated bacterium and 1,00,000–1,50,000X for the viruses).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Microbes include bacteria (which may be rod-shaped or spherical and possess flagella for motility) as well as viruses such as polyhedral Adenovirus (which causes respiratory infections) and rod-shaped Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. (I) shows a rod-shaped cell with wavy appendages, representing a flagellated rod-shaped bacterium.
2. (II) shows an icosahedral/polyhedral virus without a tail, representing Adenovirus.
3. (III) shows compact, rigid rod-shaped viruses, representing Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying each morphology against the standard microbial forms confirms that (I) is a rod-shaped bacterium with flagella, (II) is Adenovirus, and (III) is Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV).

answer.text: (I) Rod-shaped bacterium with flagella, (II) Adenovirus, (III) Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV)
(I) Rod-shaped bacterium with flagella, (II) Bacteriophage, (III) Spherical coccus bacterium
(I) Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), (II) Adenovirus, (III) Rod-shaped bacterium with flagella

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MICROBESINHUMANWELFARE_DIAGRAM_Q04 - BOD comparison of river water, sewage, and STP effluent

questiontext.text: The given bar graph shows the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) values of three water samples X, Y, and Z collected from a relatively clean river, untreated municipal sewage, and the secondary effluent discharged from a sewage treatment plant (STP). Which of the following correctly identifies X, Y, and Z?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The bar graph gives the BOD values of three water samples: Sample X has a BOD of \(400\text{ mg/L}\), Sample Y has a BOD of \(20\text{ mg/L}\), and Sample Z has a BOD of \(8\text{ mg/L}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The river water is assumed to be relatively clean compared to sewage and treated effluent, and the secondary effluent has undergone aerobic microbial treatment in a sewage treatment plant.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
BOD refers to the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria. Indirectly, BOD is a measure of the organic matter present in water: the greater the BOD of waste water, the greater is its polluting potential.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Sample X (\(400\text{ mg/L}\)) has the highest BOD, indicating the largest amount of oxidisable organic matter and highest polluting potential; hence, it corresponds to untreated municipal sewage.
2. Sample Y (\(20\text{ mg/L}\)) has a drastically reduced BOD compared to untreated sewage because aerobic microbes (flocs) consume most of the organic matter during secondary treatment; hence, it corresponds to secondary effluent from the STP.
3. Sample Z (\(8\text{ mg/L}\)) has the lowest BOD, indicating the least organic matter and lowest polluting potential; hence, it corresponds to relatively clean river water.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Ordering the samples from highest to lowest organic pollution (\(400\text{ mg/L} > 20\text{ mg/L} > 8\text{ mg/L}\)) confirms that X is untreated sewage, Y is secondary STP effluent, and Z is river water.

answer.text: X: River water, Y: Secondary STP effluent, Z: Untreated sewage
X: Secondary STP effluent, Y: Untreated sewage, Z: River water
X: Untreated sewage, Y: Secondary STP effluent, Z: River water
X: Untreated sewage, Y: River water, Z: Secondary STP effluent
